reason: The wording holds; the tag and the source line do not. I re-read the local text of the novel (yolt.txt, from the same digital copy). The epigraph page prints You only live twice: / Once when you are born / And once when you look death in the face., credited After BASHO, Japanese poet, 1643-94. It sits just before Part One and ends with a full stop. In chapter 11, Anatomy Class, Bond composes the same verse for Tiger, saying it makes as much sense as old Basho, and Tiger answers that it has the wrong number of syllables in Japanese. So Fleming wrote it and the card rightly bylines Fleming. The text was read in an unofficial copy, not the Cape 1964 page. shipped.js: not shipped, no near line, Fleming at 0 of 3, not banned. In scope: a 1964 novel. The famous film of 1967 took its title from the book, not the other way round. Publishable, and a mortality line that is not bleak. REFUTED on two correctable points. First, the tag. The work is a novel, and the Classics tags verse inside another form by the form of the work (verse in Hamlet, Brand, Mariam, Shakuntala and Oedipus at Colonus all went in as Drama), so this is Fiction, not Poetry. Second, the source line. Printed as after Bashō invites the reader to think the verse is Fleming adapting a real Basho haiku. It is not: no Basho original stands behind it, and the novel itself has Bond write it and Tiger reject it as a haiku. The Basho credit is Fleming's own conceit, and a card should not carry a false trail toward Basho, who is himself a Classics author (one line, month 8 carry). The better source names the scene rather than the fake credit, at 120 characters with no dash. It leads with the name, and the line needs no speaker because the epigraph is in the author's voice. If the editor keeps the Basho credit visible, the note should say plainly that the verse is Fleming's own, written for Bond, and that no Basho poem stands behind it.
